blocks.text:
Consider the exponential function:
\[y = a^{x}\quad (a > 0,\ a \ne 1) \quad \text{...(1)}\]
(i) Domain, Continuity, Positivity and Range of Exponential Function

Domain: The exponential function is defined for all real values of \(x\). We can substitute any real number (positive, negative, or zero) in place of \(x\), and the expression \(a^{x}\) is always meaningful. Hence, the domain of the exponential function is \(]-\infty, \infty[\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Notation: \(]-\infty, \infty[\) is the same as \((-\infty, \infty)\), the set of all real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\). A reversed bracket \(]\ \ [\) means the end point is not included, exactly like a round bracket.

Continuity: Continuity at a point \(c \in\ ]-\infty, \infty[\) is shown using the equation:
\[\lim_{x \to c} a^{x} = a^{c}\]
This shows that the exponential function is continuous on the whole domain \(]-\infty, \infty[\). Thus, the graph of the exponential function has no jump or hole.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: "Continuous" means the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. The equation says: as \(x\) gets closer to \(c\), the value \(a^{x}\) gets closer to the actual value \(a^{c}\). For example, as \(x \to 2\), \(2^{x} \to 2^{2} = 4\); there is no sudden jump.

Positivity: If \(x = n\), a positive integer, then \(a^{n} = a \cdot a \cdot \ldots \cdot a\) (\(n\) times). Since \(a > 0\), the product of positive numbers is positive. Thus \(a^{n} > 0\). Also,
\[a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}\]
Since \(a^{n} > 0\), its reciprocal is also positive. So \(a^{-n} > 0\). Moreover, \(a^{0} = 1 > 0\).

If \(x\) is rational, then \(x = \frac{p}{q}\), where \(p\) is an integer and \(q\) is a natural number. Thus:
\[a^{x} = a^{p/q} = \sqrt[q]{a^{p}}\]
From the integer case, \(a^{p} > 0\). Since the \(q^{\text{th}}\) root of a positive number is also positive, we have \(a^{p/q} > 0\).

Thus, \(a^{x} > 0\) for all rational numbers \(x\). For irrational values of \(x\), we accept that \(a^{x}\) is also positive. However, a rigorous proof of this fact is beyond the scope of this level.
Hence, \(y = a^{x} > 0\) for all real numbers \(x\). It follows that the graph of the exponential function always lies above the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Try the three cases with numbers: \(2^{3} = 8 > 0\); \(2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8} > 0\); \(8^{2/3} = \sqrt[3]{8^{2}} = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4 > 0\). Even \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-5} = 32\) is positive. A negative exponent makes the value small or large, but never negative.
Range: By observing the following facts:
We conclude that the range of the exponential function (1) is \(]0, \infty[\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why do these four facts give the whole of \(]0, \infty[\)? The values get as close to 0 as we like (fact 1 or 2), become as large as we like, and the graph has no gaps (fact 3), so every positive number in between is reached. Fact 4 says no value is 0 or negative. The symbol \(0^{+}\) means "tends to 0 from above", through positive values.
(ii) Intercepts of Exponential Function

\(y\)-intercept: To find the \(y\)-intercept, put \(x = 0\) in equation (1):
\[y = a^{0} = 1\]
So, the exponential function \(y = a^{x}\) cuts the \(y\)-axis at the point \((0, 1)\).

\(x\)-intercept: To find the \(x\)-intercept, put \(y = 0\) in equation (1):
\[a^{x} = 0\]
But \(a^{x} > 0\) for all real \(x\). It follows that there is no \(x\)-intercept.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: So every exponential graph, whatever its base, passes through the same point \((0, 1)\): \(2^{0} = e^{0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{0} = 1\). This is the first point to plot in any exponential graph.

blocks.title: Strictly Increasing and Strictly Decreasing Functions
blocks.text:
Let \(y = f(x)\) be a real-valued function and let \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in D_{f}\) be any two points such that \(x_{1} < x_{2}\). The function \(f\) is called:
(i) Strictly increasing if \(f(x_{1}) < f(x_{2})\). In this case, the graph of the function rises as \(x\) moves from left to right along the \(x\)-axis.
(ii) Strictly decreasing if \(f(x_{1}) > f(x_{2})\). In this case, the graph of the function falls as \(x\) moves from left to right along the \(x\)-axis.
For Example: Consider the function \(y = x^{2}\). This function is strictly decreasing on \(]-\infty, 0[\) and strictly increasing on \(]0, \infty[\).
(iii) Exponential Function is Strictly Increasing or Strictly Decreasing
Let \(f(x) = a^{x}\), where \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\).
Case-1: If a > 1

Let \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow x_{2} - x_{1} > 0\). Then
\[a^{x_{2}} = a^{x_{1}} \cdot a^{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
Since \(x_{2} - x_{1} > 0\) and \(a > 1\), we have \(a^{x_{2} - x_{1}} > 1\). So:
\[a^{x_{2}} = a^{x_{1}} \cdot a^{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{x_{2}} > a^{x_{1}}\]
Hence, \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow a^{x_{1}} < a^{x_{2}}\).
Therefore, \(y = a^{x}\) is strictly increasing when \(a > 1\).
Case-2: If 0 < a < 1

Let \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow x_{2} - x_{1} > 0\). Then
\[a^{x_{2}} = a^{x_{1}} \cdot a^{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
Since \(0 < a < 1\) and \(x_{2} - x_{1} > 0\), we have \(a^{x_{2} - x_{1}} < 1\). So:
\[a^{x_{2}} = a^{x_{1}} \cdot a^{x_{2} - x_{1}}\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{x_{2}} < a^{x_{1}}\]
Hence, \(x_{1} < x_{2} \Rightarrow a^{x_{1}} > a^{x_{2}}\).
Therefore, \(y = a^{x}\) is strictly decreasing when \(0 < a < 1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two facts drive this proof.
1. The law of indices \(a^{m} \cdot a^{n} = a^{m+n}\) gives \(a^{x_{1}} \cdot a^{x_{2} - x_{1}} = a^{x_{2}}\).
2. A base bigger than 1 raised to a positive power is bigger than 1 (\(2^{0.5} \approx 1.414\)); a base between 0 and 1 raised to a positive power is smaller than 1 (\(0.5^{0.5} \approx 0.707\)).
Multiplying the positive number \(a^{x_{1}}\) by something bigger than 1 makes it bigger; by something smaller than 1 makes it smaller. That is the whole proof.
(iv) Injectivity of Exponential Functions

blocks.title: Definition of Injectivity (One-to-One Function)
blocks.text:
Recall that a function \(y = f(x)\) is called injective (one-to-one) if different inputs always give different outputs. Formally, a function is one-to-one if: whenever for \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in \operatorname{Dom} f\) such that \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\), we have \(x_{1} = x_{2}\).
A function is injective if every horizontal line meets its graph at most once; equivalently, its graph is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

Let \(f(x) = a^{x}\), where \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\). Further, let \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\) for some \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in\ ]-\infty, \infty[\). So:
\[a^{x_{1}} = a^{x_{2}}\]
Case-1: If \(x_{1} < x_{2}\), then from the function \(f(x) = a^{x}\) either \(a^{x_{1}} < a^{x_{2}}\) (when \(a > 1\)) or \(a^{x_{1}} > a^{x_{2}}\) (when \(0 < a < 1\)). Which is impossible.
Case-2: If \(x_{1} > x_{2}\), then from the function \(f(x) = a^{x}\) either \(a^{x_{1}} > a^{x_{2}}\) (when \(a > 1\)) or \(a^{x_{1}} < a^{x_{2}}\) (when \(0 < a < 1\)). Which is again impossible.
Hence, we must have \(x_{1} = x_{2}\) and consequently, \(f(x) = a^{x}\) is injective. It follows that any horizontal line meets the graph of \(f(x) = a^{x}\) at most once.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Compare with \(y = x^{2}\): \(2^{2} = (-2)^{2} = 4\), two inputs with the same output, so \(x^{2}\) is not one-to-one (the line \(y = 4\) meets its graph twice). But \(2^{x} = 4\) only for \(x = 2\).
Injectivity is what lets us solve exponential equations by comparing exponents: \(2^{x} = 8 = 2^{3} \Rightarrow x = 3\). This is used in 1.10.
(v) Horizontal Asymptote of Exponential Function

Note that if \(a > 1\), then \(a^{x} \to 0^{+}\) as \(x \to -\infty\), and if \(0 < a < 1\), then \(a^{x} \to 0^{+}\) as \(x \to \infty\). It follows that the horizontal line \(y = 0\) represents the horizontal asymptote for the exponential function.

blocks.title: Note: (Horizontal Asymptote)
blocks.text:
A horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line \(y = c\) which a function approaches as \(x\) becomes very large (or very small), but the graph does not necessarily touch or cross it.
Formally the vertical line \(y = c\) is called horizontal asymptote for the function \(y = f(x)\) if \(f(x) \to c\) as \(x \to -\infty\) or \(x \to \infty\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "Formally the vertical line \(y = c\) is called horizontal asymptote". A line \(y = c\) is horizontal, not vertical. Correct: the horizontal line \(y = c\) is called a horizontal asymptote of \(y = f(x)\) if \(f(x) \to c\) as \(x \to -\infty\) or \(x \to \infty\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: See it with numbers: \(2^{-10} = \frac{1}{1024} \approx 0.001\) and \(2^{-20} \approx 0.000001\). The graph of \(2^{x}\) gets closer and closer to the \(x\)-axis on the left, but \(2^{x}\) is never 0, so it never reaches the axis. That is exactly what an asymptote is.

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = e^{x}\), an exponential function with base \(a = e \approx 2.718\).
To find: its graph.
Method: use the properties proved above for \(y = a^{x}\) (domain, range, intercept, asymptote, increasing or decreasing), then a short table of values, then join the points with a smooth curve. Since \(e > 1\), we use the case \(a > 1\).

Step 1: Domain and range
\[\text{Domain} = \mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\]
\[\text{Range} = (0, \infty)\]
Why: \(a^{x}\) is defined for every real \(x\) and \(a^{x} > 0\), with range \(]0, \infty[\) (property (i)).

Step 2: Intercepts
\[x = 0:\quad e^{0} = 1\]
The graph cuts the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 1)\); there is no \(x\)-intercept.
Why: every exponential function passes through \((0, 1)\), and \(e^{x} = 0\) has no solution because \(e^{x} > 0\) (property (ii)).

Step 3: Asymptote and monotonicity
\(y = 0\) is the horizontal asymptote, and \(f\) is continuous and strictly increasing.
Why: \(e > 1\), so \(e^{x} \to 0^{+}\) as \(x \to -\infty\) (property (v)) and \(e^{x}\) rises from left to right (property (iii), Case-1).

Step 4: Values for positive \(x\)
\[e^{1} \approx 2.718,\quad e^{2} \approx 7.389\]
\[e^{3} \approx 20.086,\quad e^{10} \approx 22026.466\]
\[e^{100} \approx 2.688 \times 10^{43}\]
Why: these show how fast \(e^{x}\) grows; as \(x \to +\infty\), \(e^{x} \to +\infty\).

Step 5: Values for negative \(x\)
\[e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e} \approx 0.368\]
\[e^{-2} \approx 0.135,\quad e^{-3} \approx 0.0498\]
\[e^{-10} \approx 0.0000454\]
\[e^{-100} \approx 3.720 \times 10^{-44}\]
Why: \(e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^{x}}\), so each value is the reciprocal of a value in Step 4: positive, small, and tending to 0 as \(x \to -\infty\), but never 0.

Step 6: Plot and join
Plot \((-2, 0.14)\), \((-1, 0.37)\), \((0, 1)\), \((1, 2.72)\), \((2, 7.39)\) and join them with a smooth rising curve that hugs the \(x\)-axis on the left without touching it (Figure 1.6).
Why: the values are rounded to two decimals for plotting; the shape follows Steps 1-3.

Check: a value and its reciprocal must multiply to 1:
\[e^{1} \times e^{-1} \approx 2.718 \times 0.368\]
\[\approx 1.000\]
Also every value in the tables is positive and the values increase with \(x\), as Steps 1 and 3 predict.
blocks.answer: The graph of \(f(x) = e^{x}\) is the smooth rising curve through \((-2, 0.14)\), \((-1, 0.37)\), \((0, 1)\), \((1, 2.72)\), \((2, 7.39)\); it lies above the \(x\)-axis and has \(y = 0\) as horizontal asymptote (Figure 1.6).

Example 7: values of \(e^{x}\) for negative \(x\) (book's table)

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\), an exponential function with base \(a = \frac{1}{2}\).
To find: its graph.
Method: the same plan as Example 7, but now \(0 < a < 1\), so we use the decreasing case.

Step 1: Domain and range
\[\text{Domain} = \mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\]
\[\text{Range} = (0, \infty)\]
Why: these hold for every exponential function \(a^{x}\) (property (i)).

Step 2: Intercept
\[x = 0:\quad \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{0} = 1\]
The graph cuts the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 1)\); no \(x\)-intercept.
Why: property (ii); \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x} > 0\) for all \(x\).

Step 3: Asymptote and monotonicity
\(y = 0\) is the horizontal asymptote; \(f\) is continuous and strictly decreasing because \(a = \frac{1}{2} < 1\).
Why: for \(0 < a < 1\), \(a^{x} \to 0^{+}\) as \(x \to \infty\) (property (v)), and property (iii), Case-2.

Step 4: Values for positive \(x\)
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{1} = 0.5,\quad \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = 0.25\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = 0.125\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{10} = \dfrac{1}{1024} \approx 0.0009766\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{100} \approx 7.89 \times 10^{-31}\]
Why: each increase of 1 in \(x\) halves the value; as \(x \to +\infty\), the value \(\to 0\).

Step 5: Values for negative \(x\)
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-x} = 2^{x}\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-1} = 2,\quad \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-2} = 4\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-3} = 8,\quad \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-10} = 1024\]
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-100} = 2^{100} \approx 1.268 \times 10^{30}\]
Why: a negative exponent turns \(\frac{1}{2}\) into its reciprocal 2; as \(x \to -\infty\), the value \(\to \infty\).

Step 6: Plot and join
Plot \((-2, 4)\), \((-1, 2)\), \((0, 1)\), \((1, 0.5)\), \((2, 0.25)\) and join them with a smooth falling curve that approaches the \(x\)-axis on the right without touching it (Figure 1.7).
Why: the shape follows Steps 1-3.

Check: \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x} = 2^{-x}\), so the value at \(x\) equals the value of \(2^{x}\) at \(-x\): for example \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2} = 4 = 2^{2}\). The graph is the mirror image of \(y = 2^{x}\) in the \(y\)-axis, which is why it falls where \(2^{x}\) rises.
blocks.answer: The graph of \(f(x) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\) is the smooth falling curve through \((-2, 4)\), \((-1, 2)\), \((0, 1)\), \((1, 0.5)\), \((2, 0.25)\); it lies above the \(x\)-axis and has \(y = 0\) as horizontal asymptote (Figure 1.7).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(y = a^{x}\ (a > 0, a \ne 1)\): domain \(]-\infty, \infty[\), range \(]0, \infty[\), continuous everywhere.
2. \(a^{x} > 0\) for every real \(x\): the graph lies above the \(x\)-axis.
3. \(y\)-intercept \((0, 1)\); no \(x\)-intercept.
4. Strictly increasing if \(a > 1\), strictly decreasing if \(0 < a < 1\); hence one-to-one.
5. \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis) is the horizontal asymptote.
6. To sketch: properties first, then a table for \(x = -2, \ldots, 2\), then a smooth curve.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Drawing the curve touching or crossing the \(x\)-axis: \(a^{x}\) is never 0 or negative.
2. Marking the asymptote on the wrong side: for \(a > 1\) the curve approaches the axis on the left; for \(0 < a < 1\), on the right.
3. Calling the asymptote \(y = 0\) a "vertical" line (as the book's note misprints): \(y = c\) is always horizontal.
4. Truncating decimals instead of rounding: \(e^{-1} \approx 0.368\), not 0.367.
